quotes.name: Joseph Cramp
quotes.quote: *(Joseph lets out a low, dry chuckle, rubbing the back of his neck with a calloused hand. He glances down at his work shoes, then back up at the reporter, his voice warm but steady.)* "First fire? Honestly, it's probably not the dramatic one folks expect. It's the supply closet inventory on the third floor of the Civic Center. That's the one that's been a slow bleed for years—nobody's kept a proper log since before I got my first set of keys. Come Monday morning, I know I'm gonna open that door and it'll look like a tornado hit a Staples. Paper towels everywhere, the good floor cleaner mixed in with the cheap stuff, and a mop bucket that's got a squeaky wheel that'll wake the dead." He shrugs, a hint of pride in his eyes. "Twenty-eight years taught me that the big fires are just a bunch of little sparks that got ignored. You don't put out a fire by yelling at it. You show up early, you check the corners, you learn which door sticks in the humidity and which tenant always leaves the back exit propped open. You take care of the small stuff so the building can breathe. That's the whole job. The title changed, but the principle didn't. You keep the place solid, and the people in it can do their thing." *(He pauses, a small smile breaking through.)* "So yeah, I'll be the guy with the clipboard and a fresh roll of trash bags on Monday. It ain't glamorous, but it's mine. And I'm ready for it."

quotes.name: Jocelyn Santo
quotes.quote: Oh, that's a good question. Let me think. One thing that's already different—really different—is the coffee situation. Travis is a pour-over guy, like, he has the little scale and the gooseneck kettle and he weighs the beans. I used to just slam a cup from a drip machine and run out the door to teach a 6 a.m. class. Now I actually sit down with him for ten minutes before I go, and it's this slow little ritual I never knew I needed. It's small, but it makes the mornings feel like ours, you know? And something we haven't worked out yet... honestly, it's the laundry. Or more specifically, the folding. I fold everything a certain way—tight, military-ish, because I grew up that way—and Travis just... balls things up and shoves them in drawers. We've had this gentle, silly standoff about it for weeks. We haven't figured it out yet. It's not a big deal, but it's the kind of thing you realize you have to actually negotiate when you merge two lives. We'll get there. Probably after I teach him my folding method one drawer at a time.
